answer.label: Not Plato — an anonymous English maxim
answer.authorDates: Anonymous English maxim · documented in print by 1908
answer.sourceLine: No work of Plato’s contains this line. It appears — unsigned — on page 560 of Tryon Edwards’ A Dictionary of Thoughts (1908 printing), directly above a separate entry that is credited “—Plato,” and the credit appears to have slid upward from one entry to the other. Wikiquote files it under “Disputed” ↗, noting it “cannot be found completely in any of his writings.”

source.excerpt:
Wise men talk because they have something to say; fools, because they would like to say something.

As empty vessels make the loudest sound, so they that have least wit are the greatest babblers.—Plato.
trail: Wikiquote’s Plato page ↗ places the saying in its Disputed section, states that it “cannot be found completely in any of his writings,” and points to A Dictionary of Thoughts (page 560) by Tryon Edwards as the source of the Plato credit.

In November 2008 the linguist Arnold Zwicky investigated the attribution in “Did Plato say this?” on Language Log ↗. A philosophy graduate student searched Plato’s works and found nothing similar; commenters noted that the pun turns on an English idiom (“have something to say” vs. “have to say something”) that would not work in Greek.

Reading the scan settles how the credit arose: on page 560 of the 1908 printing ↗ the “wise men talk” sentence is printed with no attribution at all, and the “—Plato” sits on the “empty vessels” entry immediately below it.

The nearest genuine antecedent is rhetorical rather than Platonic: Richard Whately’s Elements of Rhetoric (1858) ↗ advises a speaker to express himself “not, as if he wanted to say something, but as if he had something to say” (p. 227) — the same antithesis, decades before any dictionary of quotations pinned it on Plato.
source.excerptNote: Two separate entries, set one above the other in the left-hand column of page 560. Only the second one carries a name.

author.name: Tryon Edwards
author.heading: The man whose page the credit came from
author.metaLine: 1809–1894 · American theologian and compiler of A Dictionary of Thoughts
author.bio: Tryon Edwards was an American theologian and Congregational minister, born in Hartford, Connecticut in 1809 and died in Detroit in 1894. He served the Second Congregational Church in New London, Connecticut, but is remembered almost entirely for A Dictionary of Thoughts, the alphabetically arranged anthology of short quotations that became his best-known work. He did not write the “wise men talk” maxim and did not attribute it to anyone — his page prints it unsigned. The Plato credit belongs to the next entry down, and later readers moved it.

misattribution.heading: How this one went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a credit migrating between two adjacent lines of type — and then of the borrowed line being polished on its way around the internet.

items.why: Wikiquote lists it under “Disputed” ↗ with the note that it “cannot be found completely in any of his writings,” and Arnold Zwicky’s Language Log investigation ↗ reports that a search of Plato’s actual works turned up nothing similar.

items.who: “Wise men speak … fools because they have to say something”
items.why: The version printed in 1908 reads “Wise men talk because they have something to say; fools, because they would like to say something.” The punchier modern wording — the one people quote — is not the wording on page 560 ↗.

This is the entry that actually carries the “—Plato” on page 560, and it is frequently glued onto the first sentence as though the two were one quotation. Wikiquote notes ↗ that where Plato likens empty vessels to fools in the Symposium he says nothing about their sound, and suggests the popular saying is a conflation with a passage in the Laches.

misattribution.truthLine: On page 560 of the 1908 Dictionary of Thoughts ↗, the “wise men” sentence carries no name at all. The Plato credit belongs to the sentence printed underneath it.

context.heading: A quotation born in a column of type
lead: Books of “laconic quotations” like Tryon Edwards’ A Dictionary of Thoughts set their entries as a dense stack of short paragraphs, most signed with a dash and a name, a few left unsigned. On page 560, under the heading TALKING, an unsigned aphorism about wise men and fools happens to sit directly on top of a signed one about empty vessels. Read the block as a single quotation — which is exactly what a hurried anthologist or a copy-and-paste website does — and the “—Plato” at the bottom silently annexes the sentence above.

Arnold Zwicky, writing about this quotation on Language Log in 2008, called this the world of “folk quotation”: sayings passed hand to hand through advice manuals and anthologies, far removed from any scholarly text. One of his commenters supplied the clinching argument against a Greek origin — the joke lives entirely in an English idiom. “Have something to say” and “have to say something” are the same four words reshuffled, a symmetry that no translator of Plato could have manufactured out of Greek by accident.
detailsBody: The idea itself is not new, and it is not Plato’s either. Archbishop Richard Whately built the same antithesis into his Elements of Rhetoric, a standard nineteenth-century textbook: a writer or speaker, he advised, should seem to be expressing himself “not, as if he wanted to say something, but as if he had something to say” — advice about preaching with conviction rather than an epigram about fools. It appears on page 227 of the 1858 Morton & Griswold edition ↗.

Tryon Edwards, the compiler in whose dictionary the maxim surfaces, was an American theologian who died in 1894; the printing examined here is dated 1908. He is not the author of the line either — a dictionary of quotations gathers sayings, it does not coin them — which leaves the maxim where the evidence actually puts it: anonymous, English, and in circulation by the early twentieth century.
context.pull: The pun is made of English word order. Plato had no way to write it.
